title: Reject starlet candidate
retrievedFor: Owner request on 2026-09-12: Please review this chat and make the suggested test.

content.text: It looks to me, and I may be wrong, like the failures are mostly at the map edges where the noise is highest and the weighing towards detected astronomical flux should be low.  Is that correct?  If so, perhaps a more centrally focussed test is appropriate.

items.text:
**Your interpretation is plausible, and I agree that a centrally focused test is appropriate.** I cannot independently confirm that *most* failures are at the edges from the available report: it gives admission counts and peak amplitudes, but not their locations or local noise levels. I could not retrieve the underlying null figure or coordinate-level products here.

But you have identified a missing distinction in my previous assessment: **failure somewhere in the full map is not the same as failure to reconstruct the target in the useful POINT region.** We should investigate that before concluding that another estimator redesign is necessary.

## What your observation would change

My previous comparison of the false-model peaks with the injected source peak was incomplete. A peak of 100 in a noisy edge region and a peak of 100 in the well-measured center do not necessarily carry comparable evidence. We need their local uncertainties—and, for these spatially coherent reconstructions, the uncertainty of the relevant wavelet coefficients rather than just individual pixels. Propagating spatially varying image noise into starlet-coefficient uncertainties is an explicit part of established starlet reconstruction methods. citeturn186448view0

The reported null models remain false astronomical models. But there are two different possible diagnoses:

> **The estimator invents sources even in the well-measured target region.**

versus

> **The estimator is being allowed to reconstruct poorly constrained structure in parts of the map that should not be eligible for POINT feedback.**

The second would argue for a better-defined reconstruction domain, not necessarily a different representation. Your observation makes that a worthwhile hypothesis to test.

## There is an important wrinkle about the weights

The verification code in the Codex record shows that this candidate **did use noise weights**, estimated by wavelet band and coverage stratum. Schematically, its objective was

\[
L(m)=\frac12\sum_{(j,p)\in S}
\frac{\left[(Wm)_{j,p}-(Wy)_{j,p}\right]^2}
{\sigma_{j,p}^{\,2}},
\qquad m\geq0,
\]

where \(S\) contains the selected coefficients and \(y\) is the background-subtracted map. Unselected coefficients received zero weight.

Thus, we should not diagnose this simply as “the edge pixels were fitted with uniform weights.” The more subtle issue is that **low statistical weight does not automatically suppress the amplitude of a sufficiently flexible reconstruction.**

For example, consider fitting one freely adjustable amplitude \(a\) to one measured value \(y\):

\[
\underset{a}{\operatorname{argmin}}\;
\frac{(a-y)^2}{\sigma^2}=y.
\]

Making \(\sigma\) larger reduces the measurement’s weight, but does not change the best-fitting amplitude. Weighting suppresses its influence when it competes with other information; it does not, by itself, tell an unconstrained component to disappear.

That matters here because the optimizer could accommodate selected edge coefficients without being required to match the unselected coefficients elsewhere. **Edge-dominated noise and an insufficiently constrained reconstruction could therefore be acting together.** Restricting the useful domain could help substantially, although it would not mathematically eliminate that second issue.

Also, a correctly standardized threshold does not automatically produce fewer false selections per coefficient in high-noise regions: a \(5\sigma\) excursion is still a \(5\sigma\) excursion. The question is whether the local uncertainties are correct, whether edge regions have more opportunities for selection, and whether those selections should be eligible to generate target feedback.

## A central test is scientifically reasonable for POINT

There is already precedent in the POINT design for a configurable expected center, central search, weighted-peak initialization, and a bounded fit domain. A central-domain experiment would therefore be consistent with the intended application—not an arbitrary restriction invented solely to hide this result. fileciteturn2file0L7-L13

I would distinguish two separate restrictions:

**Measurement quality:** exclude or appropriately downweight regions whose noise or coverage makes them unsuitable for inference.

**Target location:** allow POINT feedback only within a region broad enough to contain the intended source, including the pointing errors and distorted PSFs we need to measure.

Those are different pieces of information. A low-noise feature far from the intended target may be irrelevant to POINT, while a genuine source at an allowed pointing offset should remain recoverable.

Crucially, **“centrally focused” must not mean “force the source to be centered.”** I would center the allowed search region on the commanded position, leave the recovered position free within it, and make the region large enough for the intended pointing-error range plus source extent. The small *relative* offsets between arrays do not establish a similarly small allowed *absolute* pointing error.

Nor would I simply multiply the reconstructed image by a centrally peaked weight map. That would change the inferred source morphology and flux. The restriction should enter the inference and admission policy explicitly.

## The next test I would run

I would start with the existing saved maps, not another full FRUIT campaign.

**First, quantify whether the failure really is edge-dominated.** Three measurements would answer most of the question:

| Measurement | What it distinguishes |
|---|---|
| Selected coefficients versus radius and coverage, divided by the number of eligible coefficients | Genuine edge enrichment versus simply having more searchable coefficients in the outer region |
| Reconstructed false brightness inside the proposed target region versus outside it | Harmless-to-the-central-estimate outer structure versus contamination of the useful region |
| Coefficient amplitudes divided by their assigned noise scales, separated by location and scale | Large raw excursions versus a problem with the assigned noise uncertainties |

The second measurement is particularly important. **An edge peak does not prove that the reconstruction is confined to the edge.** We need to inspect how much of the false positive model extends into the central region.

**Then run one matched central-domain variant.** Keep the wavelet transform, threshold, noise calibration, and reconstruction objective unchanged as far as possible, and change the allowed feedback domain. That would isolate your proposed explanation rather than combine it with several new ideas.

I would retain a larger surrounding map for background estimation and wavelet calculations. Wavelet coefficients depend on a neighborhood, so a central coefficient at a broad scale can still depend on noisy outer pixels. A useful central reconstruction region and the computational region needed to evaluate its coefficients are not the same thing; the starlet noise-propagation treatment likewise operates through the relevant spatial operators. citeturn186448view0

The comparison should ask whether the central variant rejects the existing null/background cases **and** recovers the compact and brighter-coma sources, including their wings. An offset-source case should check that the domain does not produce an apparently improved result by clipping the very pointing error or asymmetric structure we want to measure. Any boundary-limited result should remain explicit, consistent with the POINT design’s treatment of constrained parameters. fileciteturn2file0L14-L18

The solver failures would still need to be resolved or shown to disappear in the smaller problem. The zero-noise normalization defect is separate and should be repaired explicitly before claiming noiseless recovery. Neither issue is a reason to skip the spatial diagnosis.

**My revised recommendation is to test your edge/domain hypothesis before returning to a broader POINT-contract discussion or abandoning this starlet formulation.** The original full-domain candidate remains a failed configuration. What is not yet established—and what the available report cannot answer—is whether a physically justified, centrally restricted version can recover the target without admitting false feedback in that useful region.

Yes. The important thing is that **“reject this starlet candidate” is much narrower than “starlets were a bad idea.”** In fact, I think the experiment taught us something fairly specific about what went wrong.

The attraction of the starlet approach was sound. Starlets are designed to represent spatially coherent astronomical structure at multiple scales without imposing a Gaussian morphology; that is precisely why they are widely used for astronomical source detection and reconstruction. citeturn0search1turn0search3 The hope was that this would give us something between the extremes we had been discussing: much more morphological freedom than the Gaussian model, but substantially more coherence than independent pixels.

### What actually failed

The decisive result wasn't the solver convergence problem. It was the **null test**.

The estimator was essentially doing this:

1. Transform the map into starlet coefficients at several spatial scales.
2. Estimate the noise scale for those coefficients.
3. Identify coefficients exceeding the threshold—here roughly the familiar \(5\,\mathrm{MAD}\)-type criterion.
4. Find a positive image whose starlet transform reproduces those selected coefficients.
5. Treat that reconstructed image as candidate astronomical feedback.

That sounds reasonable. A threshold around 5σ/MAD is quite conventional in multiscale detection, although the correct threshold depends critically on the noise model and on the number/correlation of coefficients being searched. citeturn0search3turn0search6

But our experiment exposed a nasty distinction between **“there are some apparently significant coefficients”** and **“there is a coherent astronomical source.”**

In the first null realization, where the true astronomical signal is exactly zero, the method returned peaks of approximately:

| Array | False reconstructed peak | Compact test-source peak |
|---|---:|---:|
| a1100 | 104 | 100 |
| a1400 | 211 | 100 |
| a2000 | 100 | 100 |

So these weren't little noise wisps sneaking through admission. **Noise generated reconstructed objects as strong as, or stronger than, the source we were trying to recover.**

And it wasn't a fluke in one realization: 5 of 6 array/null combinations admitted something, as did all 3 background-only cases.

That's fatal for FRUIT because of the feedback loop. A false positive isn't merely an erroneous source catalog entry. We'd subtract that invented “sky” before relearning PCA; that can alter the correlated-mode estimate, which alters the next map, which may reinforce the false source. FRUIT can turn an inference error into a change in the reduction itself.

### Why did 5-MAD thresholding not protect us?

This is the most interesting result.

We have thousands of correlated coefficients at multiple scales and positions. Even fairly extreme individual excursions become considerably less remarkable when we're searching a large coefficient space. This is the general multiple-comparisons problem; false-discovery-rate approaches are one way wavelet methods explicitly address it. citeturn0search12

But there was a second, more serious problem in **our particular formulation**.

The optimization constrained the reconstruction to reproduce the **selected** starlet coefficients. It didn't sufficiently penalize what the resulting positive image did in the *unselected* parts of coefficient/image space.

So imagine noise happens to produce six apparently interesting wavelet coefficients. The optimizer asks:

> What positive image can explain these six coefficients?

It can construct a fairly substantial object that satisfies those constraints—even though most of that object's structure isn't independently demanded by the data.

That's why Codex's report says:

> “matching only the selected coefficients can produce substantial positive structure elsewhere.”

That is the key diagnosis.

It also explains why simply changing 5 MAD to 6 MAD isn't a very satisfying response. We might suppress the observed null failures, but we would be tuning the detection threshold around this particular realization without fixing the underlying inference problem.

### And the solver failures?

Those matter, but they're secondary.

All six compact-source cases and all three brighter-coma cases selected coefficients, but the reconstruction optimizer hit its 300-iteration limit. So the representation saw evidence for the injected sources, but couldn't produce an admissible reconstruction under the prescribed optimization.

That tells us something useful too: this particular starlet formulation is not only statistically permissive in the null—it is also numerically expensive. POINT is supposed to be quasi-real-time. Spending hundreds of iterations on a reconstruction that still hasn't converged is going in the wrong operational direction.

The measured timing already showed that: the 0.5-s-per-map target was exceeded on 10/25 maps. And those timings don't even represent successful full FRUIT iterations.

### The brighter-coma result is actually quite important

There had been a lingering ambiguity in our earlier RBF work: perhaps some of these sophisticated representations were failing simply because the processed POINT signal was too weak to support the inference.

The 4× coma bootstrap largely removes that excuse.

The oracle diagnostic gave processed-template scores of roughly **23.4, 15.0, and 20.1** for a1100/a1400/a2000. So there is plainly recoverable information in those processed maps. The problem isn't simply:

> “PTC destroyed the non-Gaussian source, so no clever estimator could possibly recover it.”

There's signal there.

That gives us a very useful benchmark for whatever we try next.

### Why I like the recommendation to return to the POINT reference contract

I would interpret that recommendation as **stop inventing representations for a moment and specify what information POINT actually needs FRUIT to infer.**

We've now learned quite a lot.

The independent Gaussian is too restrictive morphologically. The RBF representation is flexible and coherent, but its admission/reconstruction machinery struggled with the processed data. The positional-prior experiment demonstrated that *physical knowledge* about the arrays can be extremely powerful for rejecting contamination. And the starlet experiment demonstrated that generic multiscale sparsity by itself isn't enough to distinguish astronomical structure from noise.

That suggests to me that the next conceptual move is not “find representation #4.”

It is to write down something closer to:

**POINT feedback must infer a source that is supported by the data as an astronomical object, not merely find a flexible representation of significant map structure.**

For POINT, we actually have unusually strong prior information. There should be one compact astronomical object. Its morphology may be ugly—defocus, coma, asymmetry—but it should still have coherent spatial structure. It should appear at mutually consistent positions in all arrays, with the known small a2000 relative displacement. The amplitudes need not agree. The widths and morphology need not agree. An individual array may be too weak to contribute feedback. And importantly, the algorithm should be able to say **“there isn't enough evidence for a source”** rather than manufacture one.

That starts sounding less like an image-denoising problem and more like a **source-evidence problem followed by a reconstruction problem**.

And that distinction may be the biggest lesson from the failed starlet experiment. The literature itself generally treats multiscale support/noise modeling and object identification as distinct pieces of astronomical starlet analysis rather than assuming that thresholded coefficients automatically constitute an object. citeturn0search3 Matched filtering similarly works well precisely because it tests the data against expected coherent structure rather than testing pixels independently. citeturn0search5

So I wouldn't cross “wavelets” off the board. I would cross off:

**threshold significant starlet coefficients → positive reconstruction → call that the source.**

The starlet transform could still eventually be useful *inside* a POINT model—for example, describing departures from a compact core or quantifying multiscale residual structure. But **source existence/admission needs stronger evidence than the representation itself supplies.**

That, to me, is why this was a productive failure: it is pushing us toward separating **“is there a common astronomical object here?”** from **“how flexibly should we represent its morphology?”** Those are two different inference problems, and our last few experiments had been trying to solve both with the same machinery.
